questions.sectionHeading: Section I — Texts and Human Experiences
questions.stem: What does Andrews learn about how visiting places connects people?
questions.stimulus: Text 1 (nonfiction extract): Shawana Andrews, from HEALTH: Spirit, Country and Culture (Personal Perspectives). The text is copyright and is not reproduced here; read it in the 2025 HSC paper: https://www.nsw.gov.au/sites/default/files/noindex/2025-10/2025-hsc-english-studies.pdf
assessedOn: demonstrate understanding of human experiences in texts
analyse, explain and assess the ways human experiences are represented in texts

criteria.text: Demonstrates an effective understanding of what Andrews learns about how visiting places connects people, using appropriate supporting evidence
Demonstrates an understanding of what Andrews learns about how visiting places connects people, using some supporting evidence
Provides some relevant information about the text

questions.sampleAnswer: Andrews learns that visiting places allows people to have deeper connections to their families by creating memories. On her trip to India, Andrews and her father would visit her friends and family and be ‘offered chai and food and stay for a yarn’. Through these conversations, Andrews learnt a lot about her family. Furthermore, she says an important way to ‘transfer histories, family stories, values, lessons and ways of life’ is through visiting.

questions.stem: Explain how Vanderbilt captures the experience of learning as an adult.
questions.stimulus: Text 2 (feature article extract): Tom Vanderbilt, The joys of being an absolute beginner – for life. The text is copyright and is not reproduced here; read it in the 2025 HSC paper: https://www.nsw.gov.au/sites/default/files/noindex/2025-10/2025-hsc-english-studies.pdf
assessedOn: demonstrate understanding of human experiences in texts
analyse, explain and assess the ways human experiences are represented in texts

criteria.text: Explains effectively how Vanderbilt captures the experience of learning as an adult, using well-chosen supporting evidence
Explains how Vanderbilt captures the experience of learning as an adult, using appropriate supporting evidence
Describes how Vanderbilt captures the experience of learning as an adult, using some supporting evidence
Provides some relevant information

questions.sampleAnswer: Vanderbilt conveys the experience of learning as an adult as more challenging than learning as a child. This is shown through the anecdote of parents mocking him for learning chess with his daughter and seeing ‘kids doing the activity, and adults like me staring into their smartphones.’ The question ‘Why are adults learning chess?’ asked in a ‘mocking tone’ suggests that it is unusual for children to see adults learning new skills. Vanderbilt’s anxiety about learning is evident in his internal reflection ‘I was nervous, even though I really had nothing to lose, save my pride’, showing adults have a stronger fear of failure than children, making learning new skills more challenging.

questions.sectionHeading: Section I — Texts and Human Experiences
questions.stem: Explain how Thompson represents the experience of being at the beach.
questions.stimulus: Text 3 (poem): John Thompson, The Sun Bather. The text is copyright and is not reproduced here; read it in the 2025 HSC paper: https://www.nsw.gov.au/sites/default/files/noindex/2025-10/2025-hsc-english-studies.pdf
assessedOn: demonstrate understanding of human experiences in texts
analyse, explain and assess the ways human experiences are represented in texts

criteria.text: Explains effectively how Thompson represents the experience of being at the beach, using well-chosen supporting evidence
Explains how Thompson represents the experience of being at the beach, using appropriate supporting evidence
Describes how Thompson represents the experience of being at the beach, with some supporting evidence
Provides some relevant information about how Thompson represents the experience of being at the beach

questions.sampleAnswer: Thompson represents the experience of someone lying on the beach taking in their surroundings. ‘I spin/With nearing sleep’ metaphorically conveys the experience of the effects of the heat and surrendering to one’s senses. As the persona closes their eyes, they are ‘dissolved within’, emphasising the power of the vivid experience. Thompson further represents the sensory experience of the beach through descriptions of the ‘thundering waves’ as the sunbather ‘shield[s]’ their eyes from the bright sunlight. Also, they are aware of the ‘lads and girls/In dazzling colours’ who are enjoying themselves in the surf. The term ‘oblivion’ suggests that the immensity of this moment could be absorbed into nothingness.

questions.stem: How does Pippos portray Lucky’s sense of hope for the future?
questions.stimulus: Text 4 (prose fiction extract): Andrew Pippos, Lucky’s. The text is copyright and is not reproduced here; read it in the 2025 HSC paper: https://www.nsw.gov.au/sites/default/files/noindex/2025-10/2025-hsc-english-studies.pdf
assessedOn: demonstrate understanding of human experiences in texts
analyse, explain and assess the ways human experiences are represented in texts

criteria.text: Explains effectively how Pippos portrays Lucky’s sense of hope for the future, using well-chosen supporting evidence
Explains how Pippos portrays Lucky’s sense of hope for the future, using appropriate supporting evidence
Describes how Pippos portrays Lucky’s sense of hope for the future, using some supporting evidence
Provides some relevant information

questions.sampleAnswer: Pippos portrays Lucky’s hope for the future through the metaphor of the ship as a ‘diorama of the world’, showing that Lucky feels like the whole world is open to him. Lucky imagines Valia at various times of day, ‘working or eating’, or ‘flicking up to distance a fly’, and Pippos states that for Lucky these are ‘pleasing scenarios’. Lucky has ‘two gold rings hidden’ which are symbolic of the love and promise of marriage and hope he feels for his future with Valia in Australia. Pippos describes Circular Quay as ‘heavy with activity’ and the ‘northern shore in repose’, the contrast between action and peace reflecting Lucky’s hope for his future success in both his business and his peaceful home with Valia.

questions.sectionHeading: Section I — Texts and Human Experiences
questions.stem: How does Fidge explore the impact of role models in her childhood?
questions.stimulus: Text 5 (magazine article extract): Deirdre Fidge, Holding Out for a Hero. The text is copyright and is not reproduced here; read it in the 2025 HSC paper: https://www.nsw.gov.au/sites/default/files/noindex/2025-10/2025-hsc-english-studies.pdf
assessedOn: demonstrate understanding of human experiences in texts
analyse, explain and assess the ways human experiences are represented in texts

criteria.text: Explains in a highly effective manner how Fidge explores the impact of role models in her childhood, using detailed, well-chosen supporting evidence
Explains effectively how Fidge explores the impact of role models in her childhood, using well-chosen supporting evidence
Explains how Fidge explores the impact of role models in her childhood, with appropriate supporting evidence
Describes the impact of role models in her childhood
Provides some relevant information

questions.sampleAnswer: Fidge explores the ‘monumental’ impact that her favourite superhero, She-Ra, had in childhood through a strong, personal voice. She states that ‘She-Ra was made for me and my sister’, demonstrating the importance of diverse gender representation of role models. When describing that they were ‘desperate to see… women doing anything remotely interesting’, Fidge uses humour to emphasise the importance of seeing role models on television in childhood that resonated with her desire to see ‘strong women’ being represented doing aspirational things. When She-Ra was taken off the air, Fidge and her sister protested by writing ‘letters to the station to express our disappointment’. Her letter is a small act of protest where she exclaims, ‘Put back She-Ra. Do it… NOW!!’ where the imperative voice demonstrates the impact of having a superhero role model as it gave the author ongoing confidence to communicate her opinion with the hope of making change.
